Checklist for Equitable Data Selection for Women’s Healthcare

There are a number of elements that impact women’s health, yet data scientists and model developers are not always aware of these elements when doing research. The following checklist aims to explain dataset elements which impact women’s health and is based on clinicians perceptions of women’s health (Heaney et al. 2025). The method of translation is outlined in Heaney et al. (2026).

If you have any feedback on this checklist I would love to hear it Feedback Form

Tick off each item as you go. Your progress is saved in your browser.

Necessities

Contain both male and female patients (if condition being studied affects both)

You may wish to compare women’s data vs men’s data, as they can have different symptoms, treatment options and difference in prevalence of condition.

Contains a range of participant ages

Women can have different treatment plans/differential diagnosis based on their age.

Is it a recent dataset or could recent advancements in the condition being studied limit how old the dataset can be

Women’s health has progressed in the last number of years both in treatment options and knowledge of how symptoms present in women and men. Consider how old your dataset can be given recent advancements. This checklist was developed based on opinions of clinicians in 2023, there may be additional time-related elements to consider.

Where was the data gathered

This checklist is based off European clinicians perspectives, there may be country and government specific elements to consider.

Sex Specific Factors

Are women specific stages such as menstruation and menopause included?

Menstruation and menopause can impact chronic diseases. Changes in menstruation can indicate underlying health conditions. Similarly ‘menstuation conditions’ such as Endometriosis, PCOS/PMOS can increase the likelihood chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes (Naeem et al. 2025, Kvaskoff2015). However many clinical trials, cohort studies and animal model work with non-reproductive aims rarely include menstrual information (Vollmar et al. 2025)

Is pregnancy status known?

Pregnancy can trigger autoimmune diseases (Muller et al. 2001), worsen/improve some conditions (Merz et al. 2022). Pregnancy can impact medication options (Wang et al. 2024).

Is history of pregnancy complications known?

Events that happen during pregnancy such as ‘preaclamsia’ or ‘gestational diabeties’ can be indicators of a patients health in the future (Rajendran et al. 2023).

Does your dataset include transgendered patients?

Be aware if there are trans patients in your dataset, particularly in the pre-processing stage when you are removing any any rows with inconsistencies. Trans men may still need “women’s health” services and they may be included in these datasets (Sbragia and Vottero 2020).

Are there conditions that affect more women/men present in the dataset?

There are conditions that affect more women then men (and vice versa) this may impact the representation in your datasets Johnston and Dagar (2020). Consider what an equitable split may look like.

Clinician Information

Is the sex of the clinician known?

The sex of the clinician may impact the care women receive McKinlay et al. (2007) . Consider female patients may only feel comfortable with female clinicians.

Is the specialisation of the clinician know?

The specialisation of the clinician may impact the type of treatment the patient has access to Horne et al. (2001).

Patient Specific Factors

Is there a need to consider comorbidities?

Some comorbidities are more common in women.(Minen et al. 2016, Pahwa2023) The presence of some comorbidities will impact treatment plans.

Are pain scales present/necessary?

Women experience pain differently to men Osborne and Davis (2022). Clinicians responding to a clinical scenario of a patient in pain, rated female patients as having a less intense pain (lower pain score) than a male patient with the same description of pain (Guzikevits et al. 2024). Consider this if pain scales are in your data and indeed if they are necessary for your model.

Is ethnicity known?

Many patients face ethnic disparities when accessing care (Wheeler and Bryant 2017).

Are cultural factors known?

A woman’s culture may impact their wants/needs in medication and treatment plans, e.g. some cultures are not comfortable stopping periods completely or being on a form of birth control or may not talk about menstruation (Hennegan et al. 2019) Similarly women in some cultures may may only be able to see female clinicians (Opara et al. 2024)

Is the location known (of the patient)?

The patients location impacts their access to services. Location can be a proxy variable e.g. for socioeconomic status.

Are there personal patient factors e.g. carer responsibilities, history of abuse?

Carer responsibilities (Arksey and Hirst 2005) and abuse (Papas et al. 2023) can reduce a patients ability to be seen medically and therefor these patients may not be represented in your data.

Are there treatment plans/medication known?

Treatment plans and medication can vary based on the sex and gender of the patient. Women are less likely to be prescribed e.g. statins (Virani et al. 2015) and pain medication (Samulowitz et al. 2018). Teratogenic (i.e. could cause harm to a foetus) prohibited in pregnancy (Wang et al. 2024) and some teratogenic only available with a Pregnancy Prevention Programme (London 2025)

Is the length of diagnosis known?

Women on average take longer to get a diagnosis then men (Sun et al. 2023), be aware of this if you plan on considering diagnostic length. If your data was collected during a set time frame there may be women in your data who were diagnosed after the data collection period, or they may be removed since they didn’t have a diagnosis yet.

Domain Knowledge - i.e. knowledge of the area being studied?

Is there known gender or sex differences in the studied condition(s)?

There are conditions where women and men have different treatment options, different side effects to medication, different symptoms.

Is there additional resources to bridge the data science to medical science gap?

Some datasets can be difficult to interpret, well documented datasets, domain experts who work in the area are a great resource.

Is there a lot of background knowledge needed to understand the data?

Ensure all columns are understood and how they interact with each other. Particulary how they relate to women.

Is there domain experts to call upon who know the data?

A ‘Domain expert’ is anyone who knows the medical intricacies of the researched condition. They can help with unclear results and explain condition in dept for example: doctors, biomedical scientist, clinical nurse specialists
